title: Architecture
text: This page describes how SimilaritySearchEngine.jl is put together: its module map, the engine type hierarchy that replaces name/enum-based dispatch with real Julia types, the staging-vs-indexing split that lets a project decouple insertion from the expensive graph-connection/encoding step (dense and full-text alike), the concurrency model that lets searches run in parallel while staying safe from concurrent inserts, and the RocksDB-column-families-plus-one-mmap-file layout that makes persistence incremental instead of a single ever-growing blob.

title: Architecture
text:
Module map
The package is five source files, four of them real submodules (Schema, Project, IndexEngine, Persistence) plus embedded.jl, which defines EmbeddedEngine and the top-level functions (create_project, append_items!, search, …) directly in the SimilaritySearchEngine module itself — the friendly surface a script actually calls.





flowchart LR
    Schema["Schema<br/><small>MetadataRecord (_id, doc_id,<br/>keywords, refs), meta split</small>"]
    Project["Project<br/><small>ProjectManager, metadata CRUD</small>"]
    IndexEngine["IndexEngine<br/><small>AbstractSearchEngine hierarchy</small>"]
    Persistence["Persistence<br/><small>EngineStore, AdjacencyStore, ...</small>"]
    Embedded["embedded.jl<br/><small>EmbeddedEngine + top-level API</small>"]
    Caller(["Julia script, or<br/>SimilaritySearchServer"])

    Schema --> Project
    Schema --> Embedded
    Project --> Embedded
    IndexEngine --> Embedded
    Persistence --> Embedded
    Embedded --> Caller






IndexEngine and Persistence are deliberately independent of Project/Schema and of each other: IndexEngine knows nothing about RocksDB (its persistence hook is a plain (index, sp, ep) -> nothing callback), and Persistence knows nothing about metadata schemas or search engines (it stores plain Julia values under string keys). embedded.jl is the one place that wires all four together — every other module could, in principle, be reused on its own.
Schema/Project have no per-project typed-field schema to declare anymore: every project has exactly the same fixed-shape Schema.MetadataRecord (_id, doc_id, keywords, refs) plus a free-form meta JSON blob for everything else appended with an item — _id is the internal, sequential, always-present handle (the same id space the engine’s own vector/text store uses); doc_id is the caller’s own external id, if any; keywords/refs are the only two fields with a secondary index (Project’s fixed idx_keywords/idx_refs column families), everything else lives in meta, looked up straight from Project, never indexed.

title: Architecture
text:
Engine type hierarchy
Every index kind (SearchGraph, ExhaustiveSearch/ParallelExhaustiveSearch, BM25InvertedFile, InvertedFile) gets its own concrete engine struct, each carrying only the state that kind actually needs. There is no enum tag or string name anywhere in this hierarchy — the concrete Julia type itself is what add_item!, search_live, restore_engine, and every other generic function dispatch on.





classDiagram
    class AbstractSearchEngine {
        <<abstract>>
    }
    class SearchGraphEngine {
        index: SearchGraph
        ctx: SearchGraphContext
        minrecall: Union~Nothing, Float32~
        opt_beamsearch: OptBeamSearch
        search_ctx_pool: ContextPool
        deleted_ids: Set~UInt32~
        lock: ReadWriteLock
    }
    class GenericEngine~IndexType~ {
        index: IndexType
        ctx: Any
        search_ctx_pool: ContextPool
        deleted_ids: Set~UInt32~
        lock: ReadWriteLock
    }
    class BM25Engine {
        index: Union~Nothing, BM25InvertedFile~
        profile: Union~Nothing, TextProfile~
        textconfig: TextConfig
        variants: Union~Nothing, Dict~
        staged: Vector~String~
        ctx: InvertedFileContext
        search_ctx_pool: ContextPool
        deleted_ids: Set~UInt32~
        lock: ReadWriteLock
    }
    class InvertedFileEngine {
        index: Union~Nothing, TextInvertedFile~
        profile: Union~Nothing, TextProfile~
        textconfig: TextConfig
        variants: Union~Nothing, Dict~
        distance: PreMetric
        staged: Vector~String~
        ctx: InvertedFileContext
        search_ctx_pool: ContextPool
        deleted_ids: Set~UInt32~
        lock: ReadWriteLock
    }
    AbstractSearchEngine <|-- SearchGraphEngine
    AbstractSearchEngine <|-- GenericEngine
    AbstractSearchEngine <|-- BM25Engine
    AbstractSearchEngine <|-- InvertedFileEngine






A few design choices worth calling out:

GenericEngine{IndexType} covers ExhaustiveSearch/ParallelExhaustiveSearch (and any future dense index with no engine-specific state) with a single struct parameterized by the wrapped index type, instead of one struct per index kind.
minrecall/opt_beamsearch only exist on SearchGraphEngine — only a SearchGraph autotunes a BeamSearch toward a target recall.
BM25Engine and InvertedFileEngine each carry their whole text model in one field, profile::Union{Nothing, TextProfile} — vocabulary and weights (profile.model) plus the corpus-produced artifacts (stopword set, lemma map, query-expansion network) and the lineage saying how it was produced. That replaces the voc/model pair they carried before TextSearch 1.1 published TextProfile, and the reason to prefer it is structural: an artifact has exactly one home, and the TextConfig the tokenizer runs is derived from the profile, so an index cannot end up tokenizing documents through a different lemma map than the one it saves.
A text engine is created from an AbstractTextModelSpec: three answers to “where does the vocabulary come from”, not variations on one setting. BaseProfile(profile) trains it at creation. DefaultProfile(:es) and FitFromCorpus(textconfig; …) leave it untrained and store the recipe in fitspec, for the first index! call to carry out — the first by loading the published profile for that language and refitting it against the staged corpus, the second by delegating a fit of it to TextSearch.fit_profile. index === nothing exactly while profile === nothing. There is no separate training entry point: add_item!/append_items! always just stage raw text into staged (never an error, trained or not — see “Staging vs. indexing” below).
Fitting is the library’s job, not this package’s. train_profile is a dispatcher over the two deferred specs and nothing more: one calls TextSearch.fit_profile, the other TextSearch.load_profile + TextSearch.refit_profile. This package used to fit a vocabulary and weights itself, and every line of that was a second implementation of something the library does. What delegation costs is that a fit is now the full pipeline — LSI, expansion network, lemma clustering — with no cheap variant, which is why FitFromCorpus caps its sample at max_documents and why the recommended path avoids fitting altogether.
create_engine requires the spec and refuses nothing, and the dense kinds refuse a spec rather than ignoring one. Both directions are deliberate. The fit-from-corpus form freezes the vocabulary at the first index! call, so every term a later batch introduces is dropped from then on — nothing about the project’s behaviour afterwards distinguishes “I chose this” from “I never said”, which is exactly why it cannot be a default. In the other direction, a text model handed to an index of vectors has no reading under which it does anything, so swallowing it is how a project ends up not being the kind its author thought it was. Each spec is a type carrying its own options, so an option that only means something on one path cannot be handed to the other — the same reason this hierarchy discriminates on concrete types instead of an enum tag.
variants caches the orthographic variant map a query is bridged with (musica → música). It is a pure function of the frozen vocabulary, so it is derived once, the moment profile is set, rather than per query — deriving it costs ~0.24s over a half-million-token vocabulary, and doing it up front also keeps search_live free of any write to the engine, so it stays safe under a plain read lock. It is not persisted: reopening a project re-derives it from the restored vocabulary.
Every kind shares three fields regardless of what else it carries: deleted_ids::Set{UInt32} (logically deleted document ids — UInt32 uniformly, matching the id type search results actually come back as), lock::ReadWriteLock, and search_ctx_pool::ContextPool (see below).

title: Architecture
section: Staging vs. indexing: every engine kind has the split except exact search
text:
Staging vs. indexing: every engine kind has the split except exact search
append_items!/add_item! only ever stages an item — for SearchGraphEngine, BM25Engine, and InvertedFileEngine alike; search_live/ftsearch/allknn/fft/ closestpairs/bichromatic_kclosestpairs only ever see items an explicit index! call has actually processed, not merely staged. GenericEngine (ExhaustiveSearch/ParallelExhaustiveSearch) is the one exception: it always evaluates directly against db, so append_items!/add_item! indexes it synchronously and it has no index! method of its own.
SimilaritySearch.jl’s own SearchGraph separates staging raw vectors into its database from the (expensive) graph-connection work, and this package extends that same split to the two inverted-file text engines, which have no such native support of their own to lean on:

SearchGraphEngine: insert_dense!(index::SearchGraph, ctx, item) = push_item!(index.db, item) only ever appends item to index.db — cheap, and durable the instant it happens (see Persistence below), but index.adj (the graph itself) is untouched. IndexEngine.index!(engine::SearchGraphEngine) is the explicit, idempotent step that actually builds graph connections for whatever has been staged since the last call (or since creation) — it delegates to SimilaritySearch.index!(engine.index, engine.ctx), which itself only ever processes the backlog (length(engine.index)+1:length(database(engine.index))), so calling it repeatedly, or with nothing new staged, is a cheap no-op.
BM25Engine/InvertedFileEngine: add_item! just pushes raw text onto engine.staged — the text-engine counterpart of index.db, since TextSearch.jl’s inverted-file types have no raw-item staging area of their own to reuse. IndexEngine.index!(engine) (no corpus argument) catches up the exact same backlog range ((engine.index === nothing ? 0 : length(engine.index))+1:length(engine.staged)), encoding each staged text (bagofwords for BM25; for the weighted engine, handing the text straight to TextInvertedFile, whose own push_item! vectorizes through the profile’s model) and push_item!ing it into the real index — with one extra twist on its first call for a project created without a profile: since neither index kind can even be constructed without a Vocabulary, that call runs the engine’s fitspec over what is staged so far and builds the real index against the resulting TextProfile, before running the same backlog loop. Every later call is a plain catch-up, identical in shape to SearchGraphEngine’s.
A project created from a BaseProfile skips that entirely, and the difference is not only when the work happens: a vocabulary fitted from a sample of the first batch is frozen there, so every term appended later that it never saw is out-of-vocabulary and silently dropped. Starting from a profile fitted over the language — DefaultProfile(:es), or a BaseProfile of one you hold — is what makes an incrementally-grown text project behave.

This decouples when an item becomes durable (immediately, on append_items!) from when it becomes searchable (only after an explicit index!), so a caller controls when the expensive graph-connection/encoding cost is paid — once per big batch, on a schedule, or right before the next round of queries — instead of paying it synchronously on every single insert the way GenericEngine still does.

title: Architecture
text:
Concurrency model
None of the four underlying index kinds tolerates a search running concurrently with an insertion into the same index — a search reading index.adj/index.db while add_item! resizes/appends to those same arrays is exactly the kind of concurrent read-during-mutation none of them are built for. But all four do safely support running multiple searches concurrently against the same index, since that is exactly what their own searchbatch/allknn parallel paths already rely on internally.

ReadWriteLock
Each engine’s lock is a custom reader/writer lock (built from a Threads.Condition plus a reader count), not a plain ReentrantLock: search_live/current_beamsearch take it as a read lock (any number of readers concurrently), while add_item!/index!/ mark_deleted!/calibrate! take it as a write lock (exclusive of every reader and every other writer).





sequenceDiagram
    participant S1 as search_live (thread 1)
    participant S2 as search_live (thread 2)
    participant W as add_item! (thread 3)
    participant L as engine.lock

    S1->>L: read_lock (readers 0 to 1)
    S2->>L: read_lock (readers 1 to 2)
    Note over S1,S2: both searches run concurrently
    W->>L: write_lock (blocks: readers > 0)
    S1->>L: release (readers 2 to 1)
    S2->>L: release (readers 1 to 0)
    L->>W: write lock granted
    Note over W: insert_dense! / push_item! using engine.ctx
    W->>L: release






A read-to-write “upgrade” on the same logical operation would deadlock (the write lock waits for the reader count to hit zero, including the reader this same call is itself holding) — so a SearchGraphEngine’s minrecall-driven auto-calibrate! inside search_live is always resolved before the read lock is acquired, never nested inside it.


ContextPool
Guarding the index data isn’t enough by itself: SearchGraphContext/GenericContext/ InvertedFileContext are all mutable, reused scratch spaces (beam buffers, visited-vertices state, per-batch cost counters, …), and two concurrent searches sharing the same context object corrupt each other’s scratch state — confirmed directly by a segfault inside SearchGraph’s own beam search when two threads raced on a shared context.
ContextPool avoids both bad alternatives — sharing one context (unsafe) and allocating a fresh one on every single call (wasteful, since these contexts are non-trivial to allocate) — by handing each concurrent search_live call its own checked-out context, returned to the pool when done:





flowchart LR
    A["search_live call"] --> B{"pool.available<br/>non-empty?"}
    B -- yes --> C["pop! an idle context"]
    B -- no --> D["deepcopy(pool.template)"]
    C --> E["run the search with this context"]
    D --> E
    E --> F["checkin!: push! back onto pool.available"]






The pool grows lazily to (and then stays at) however many concurrent searches an engine has actually seen at once — never pre-allocated speculatively, never shrunk either. ctx itself (the engine’s own field) is never touched by search_live; it stays reserved for insertion, which already runs under an exclusive write_lock, so sharing it there is safe.

title: Architecture
section: Persistence: one storage unit per concern
text:
Persistence: one storage unit per concern
Earlier iterations of this design re-serialized the entire engine state — including the whole index — on every mutation. The current design instead gives each kind of state its own RocksDB column family (or, for a SearchGraph’s raw vectors, its own file outside RocksDB entirely — see below), so a mutation only ever rewrites the storage it actually touched.





flowchart TB
    subgraph db["one RocksDB directory per project"]
        records[("records<br/><small>_id → MetadataRecord (fixed shape)</small>")]
        meta[("meta<br/><small>_id → free-form meta (JSON)</small>")]
        oplog[("op_log")]
        idxkw[("idx_keywords<br/><small>keyword → _ids</small>")]
        idxrefs[("idx_refs<br/><small>referenced doc_id → _ids</small>")]
        engine[("engine <small>(ENGINE_CF)</small><br/><small>one key per engine struct field</small>")]
        adj[("searchgraph_adj <small>(ADJACENCY_CF)</small><br/><small>object_id → direct neighbors</small>")]
        stagedtext[("staged_text <small>(STAGED_TEXT_CF)</small><br/><small>append-only raw, not-yet-encoded text blocks</small>")]
        sparsedb[("sparse_db <small>(INVFILE_DB_CF)</small><br/><small>append-only encoded object blocks</small>")]
    end
    mmapfile[["dense_vectors.mmapdb<br/><small>-- not RocksDB --<br/>one row per staged vector</small>"]]

    ProjectManager -- "put_metadata! / get_metadata" --> records
    ProjectManager -- "get_meta / get_raw_meta" --> meta
    ProjectManager -- "secondary lookups" --> idxkw
    ProjectManager -- "secondary lookups" --> idxrefs
    EngineStore -- "save_field! / load_field" --> engine
    AdjacencyStore -- "save_neighbors! / load_neighbors" --> adj
    StagedTextStore -- "append_staged_texts! / load_staged_text_blocks" --> stagedtext
    InvertedFileObjectStore -- "append_objects! / load_object_blocks" --> sparsedb
    append_items_dense["append_items!<br/>(SearchGraph)"] --> mmapfile
    append_items_text["append_items!<br/>(BM25InvertedFile/InvertedFile)"] --> stagedtext






Every RocksDB column family above lives in the same directory/connection as the project’s metadata store (Project.ProjectManager.db) — Project.open_project’s extra_cf_names keyword is how IndexEngine’s persistence layer gets its own column families listed alongside Project’s, since every column family that exists on disk must be named at opendb time on every open, not only the first. dense_vectors.mmapdb is the one exception: a plain file, alongside (not inside) the RocksDB directory – raw text has no fixed-size-record shape to exploit that way, so staged_text stays a RocksDB column family, structured exactly like sparse_db (append-only, blocks keyed by starting position) but holding raw, un-encoded text instead of already-encoded objects.

EngineStore: per-field keys, not one blob
EngineStore is a field_name::Symbol => value map, one RocksDB key per struct field. save_field!/load_field touch exactly one key; save_fields! is only used for rare, one-shot multi-field transitions (right after create_engine, or the moment a text engine’s vocabulary is first trained). A soft delete only ever rewrites :deleted_ids; a calibrate! call only ever rewrites :opt_beamsearch.


Dense vectors: a memory-mapped file, not a RocksDB column family
A SearchGraphEngine’s raw vectors are fixed-dimension Float32 data — exactly what SimilaritySearch.MMapMatrixDatabase is for, and its own append-only counter/growth/fsync discipline already gives durable, in-order, crash-safe storage with no need for RocksDB’s batch-keying scheme, at a much cheaper per-vector read than a RocksDB point lookup (confirmed empirically against VectorDatabase/BlockMatrixDatabase in SimilaritySearch.jl’s own test suite). append_items! writes staged vectors directly into this file, at stage time — not through CallbackLog at all, unlike everything else in this section — since a vector is durable-worthy the moment it’s staged, long before any graph-linking work happens. The file (dense_vectors.mmapdb) is created lazily, on the first dense append, since its dimension isn’t known before then.
Batch size matters a lot here: MMapMatrixDatabase fsyncs once per append_items! call, never per individual vector, so the number of calls a caller makes (not the total vector count) drives wall-clock time — confirmed empirically, 200,000 128-dim vectors as one 200,000-item call took ~0.10s; the same total split into calls of 10 items took ~2.1s; one call per single item measured roughly 1000x slower than the all-at-once case. Prefer fewer, larger append_items! calls over many small ones.


Incremental adjacency/posting-list persistence: different shapes, by necessity
The graph/posting-list structure itself is the other expensive, ever-growing part, so it is never saved as a single value either. Its incremental format is driven by SimilaritySearch.CallbackLog, an observer that fires a flush(index, sp, ep) callback on every :add! event a mutating call reports — SimilaritySearch.jl standardizes every index kind’s structural events onto this one name, regardless of which entry point triggered it, and the observation channel carries nothing else, so CallbackLog never has to branch on the event itself. What does differ by index kind is the shape of what gets saved, and when this callback fires relative to append_items!.





sequenceDiagram
    participant Caller as index!(handle)
    participant Idx as SearchGraph
    participant CB as CallbackLog
    participant ES as EngineStore
    participant AS as AdjacencyStore

    Note over Caller,Idx: append_items! already staged vectors into<br/>dense_vectors.mmapdb -- no CallbackLog involved
    Caller->>Idx: SimilaritySearch.index!(engine.index, ctx)
    Idx->>Idx: build graph connections for the staged backlog (range sp:ep)
    Idx->>CB: LOG(:add!, index, ctx, sp, ep)
    Note right of Idx: fires BEFORE connect_reverse_links!<br/>index.adj[sp:ep] holds only direct links
    CB->>AS: save_neighbors!(i, direct_neighbors(i)) for i in sp:ep
    CB->>ES: save_field!(:graph_len, ep)
    Idx->>Idx: connect_reverse_links! (in memory only)






For a SearchGraph, LOG fires before connect_reverse_links! runs for that range — so what’s captured at that instant is exactly the direct-links-only slice. This is by design, not a bug to route around: connect_reverse_links! isn’t idempotent (re-running it on an already-complete graph would duplicate reverse edges), so the on-disk format never saves reverse links at all. :graph_len (how far graph-indexing actually got, which can lag behind how many vectors are staged in dense_vectors.mmapdb if the process closed between an append_items! and its follow-up index!) lets reloading resume exactly where indexing left off, over the same, already-fully-restored .db.
BM25InvertedFile/InvertedFile have no direct/reverse-link hazard: their own LOG only fires after a push_item! call’s mutation is fully done, so InvertedFileObjectStore simply appends the raw encoded objects just inserted (invertedfile_objects) as a new block. LOG here fires from inside an index! call’s backlog loop (see “Staging vs. indexing” above) rather than from append_items! directly — append_items! only ever writes to StagedTextStore, the raw-text counterpart of dense_vectors.mmapdb; sparse_db’s already-encoded blocks only grow once an index! call actually catches the backlog up. Reloading index itself still rebuilds the whole thing by replaying every saved encoded object back through the library’s own push_item! — a rebuild-by-reinsertion design, not a real on-disk posting-list format — while staged (every raw text ever staged, whether or not it’s been encoded yet) is restored separately, straight from StagedTextStore, and handed to restore_engine alongside object_blocks. This is a deliberate scaling limit, not an oversight: it’s fine up to a few million documents, since the whole corpus and the whole rebuilt index have to fit in memory and reloading costs the full original indexing time again. It is not a design for billion-document corpora, which need genuinely disk-backed, paged-on-demand posting lists.
GenericEngine (ExhaustiveSearch/ParallelExhaustiveSearch) has no incremental format of its own — its on_change just flags pending_flush[], and embedded.jl saves the whole index as a single :index value right after the triggering add_item! call returns. This is acceptable for these exact, in-memory-only index kinds, which have no adjacency or posting-list structure to split apart in the first place, and index synchronously on every add_item! same as the text engines.


Reopening a project





sequenceDiagram
    participant Caller as open_project
    participant MM as dense_vectors.mmapdb
    participant ES as EngineStore
    participant AS as AdjacencyStore
    participant IE as IndexEngine

    Caller->>ES: load_field(:kind)
    Caller->>MM: open_dense_vectors(dir) → vector_blocks (one block, every staged vector)
    Caller->>AS: load_neighbors(i) for i in 1:graph_len
    Caller->>ES: load_field(:graph_len, 0)
    Caller->>IE: build_searchgraph(distance, vector_blocks, load_neighbors, graph_len)
    IE->>IE: replay every staged vector into index.db (in full)
    IE->>IE: add! each of the first graph_len objects' saved direct neighbors
    IE->>IE: connect_reverse_links! once, over 1:graph_len
    IE-->>Caller: reconstructed SearchGraph -- index.len[] = graph_len
    Caller->>IE: restore_engine(state, on_change) → SearchGraphEngine






graph_len can be <= length(index.db): every staged vector is always fully restored into .db (that’s durable from the moment it was staged), but only the first graph_len of them were ever graph-indexed before the project last closed — if it closed between an append_items! and its follow-up index! call, the gap is restored as staged-but-not-yet- searchable, waiting on a future index!(handle) call to catch it up, exactly as it was before closing.
restore_engine dispatches on state.kind exactly the way create_engine dispatches on an index type. IndexEngine.extra_state_fields(kind) only covers GenericEngine’s wrapped index types (ExhaustiveSearch/ParallelExhaustiveSearch) — the static, per-kind list of extra EngineStore keys open_project’s generic fallback branch reads back before an engine instance exists to ask snapshot_state directly. SearchGraphEngine/ BM25Engine/InvertedFileEngine are deliberately not covered by it: each needs its own dedicated combination of EngineStore fields (:minrecall/:opt_beamsearch for SearchGraphEngine; :profile/:fitspec for BM25Engine; those two plus :distance for InvertedFileEngine) plus its own dedicated block-store reads (vector_blocks/ load_neighbors/graph_len for SearchGraphEngine; object_blocks/staged for the two text engines) assembled by hand, directly in open_project, rather than a generic per-kind field list.

title: Architecture
section: Logging: informative output and persistence are independent
text:
Logging: informative output and persistence are independent
Every engine’s context carries two logging slots, and that split is what makes the independence structural instead of a convention to remember. This engine used to hand-roll it — one slot holding three backends of two different kinds, with a comment explaining which of them could affect persistence — until SimilaritySearch.jl grew the distinction itself.

ctx.reporters — where progress goes to be read. Always at least one InformativeLog printing a throttled status line to stderr; a log_io adds a second one writing the same line to any caller-given IO (an open file handle, or stdout/stderr). Purely informative, and it cannot be anything else: a reporter is only ever handed a message.
ctx.observers — what reacts to a structural change. A CallbackLog here forwards every :add! report, untouched by any throttling, to whatever on_change closure embedded.jl installed. This is the actual persistence trigger.






flowchart LR
    Mutation["push_item! / append_items!"] --> INFORM["INFORM<br/>(ctx.reporters)"]
    Mutation --> OBSERVE["OBSERVE :add!<br/>(ctx.observers)"]
    INFORM --> Stderr["InformativeLog<br/>→ stderr, throttled"]
    INFORM --> FileIO["InformativeLog(log_io)<br/>→ any IO, throttled<br/>(optional)"]
    OBSERVE --> CallbackLog["CallbackLog<br/>→ on_change(index, sp, ep)<br/>(persistence trigger)"]






The two channels cannot interfere. Silencing the console is reporters=[], and persistence continues untouched; conversely no observer can be lost by turning output down, because turning output down does not reach that slot.

title: Architecture
text:
Soft deletes
mark_deleted! adds a document’s id to deleted_ids and nothing else — the underlying index is never touched, so no rebuild or backfill is needed. search_live reports a deleted flag per candidate instead of silently dropping deleted candidates and backfilling with the next-best live one: compensating for deletions by overfetching would have to grow with the total number of deletions, and it would hide from the caller which ids were even considered. A caller that wants k live results after filtering is expected to page for more (e.g. via a cursor over successive top-k' windows) at a layer above this one — SimilaritySearchServer, not this package.

title: Architecture
text:
Whole-dataset operations
allknn, fft, closestpairs, and bichromatic_kclosestpairs all run synchronously, in-process, directly against a dense project’s index — no job queue, unlike the HTTP API’s POST /api/v1/jobs/allknn. Each does real work proportional to the whole dataset (or two datasets, for the bichromatic case): allknn is every item’s own top-k neighbors at once; fft (Farthest-First-Traversal) picks k well-separated items for diverse sampling; closestpairs finds the k globally closest pairs within one project (near-duplicate/echo detection); bichromatic_kclosestpairs finds the k closest pairs between a project’s own index and a second, unindexed collection of vectors. All four require a dense (SearchGraphEngine) project that’s had index! run at least once — none apply to a text project.

title: Architecture
text:
Where this leaves SimilaritySearchServer
This package covers project lifecycle, core CRUD, calibration, and the whole-dataset operations above. Pagination policy over soft-deleted results, HTTP/CLI surfaces, job queues, and telemetry all live one layer up, in the sibling SimilaritySearchServer package, which depends on this one and is kept in sync with it as this package’s design settles.

title: Paragraph search over books and Wikipedia
text:
This is the tutorial to read after Getting started. That one used one novel and took every default; this one uses four real corpora, in three languages, each indexed against a text model fitted for it — which is where the decisions that matter start mattering.
Paragraphs, not documents. A search here answers with the paragraph that contains the answer, not with the book it appears in. That choice runs all the way down: it is the unit the corpora are built in, the unit the profiles are fitted on, and the unit the projects index. Retrieving whole books would be close to useless — Moby-Dick is “about” almost anything you can ask — and it is also a worse model, because a document frequency computed over books says nothing (nearly every word is in nearly every book) while one computed over paragraphs is informative.

title: Paragraph search over books and Wikipedia
text:
Before you start
Everything below reads what tutorials/prepare.jl builds. That script downloads the books, extracts the Wikipedia articles, fits a profile per corpus and indexes each into a project. It is measured in tens of minutes and hundreds of megabytes, which is exactly why it is a script and not a section of this page:
# from the repository root
julia --project=tutorials tutorials/prepare.jl            # the documented scale, ~1 hour
julia --project=tutorials tutorials/prepare.jl --smoke    # a few books and articles, ~5 minutes
Each step (corpora, profiles, projects) is separately runnable and caches to disk, so a run that fails halfway resumes instead of restarting.






NoteRendering this page yourself



Quarto’s Julia engine needs a writable runtime directory. On a machine where /run/user/$UID is not writable, quarto render fails with PermissionDenied ... mkdir '/run/user/…/julia' before running a single cell. Point it somewhere else:
XDG_RUNTIME_DIR=$(mktemp -d) quarto render manual

title: Paragraph search over books and Wikipedia
text:

Two things in that table are worth pausing on.
Wikipedia yields far more paragraphs per article than you would expect. title: Paragraph search over books and Wikipedia
text:
Profiles
A text project needs to know how to turn text into tokens and how to weight them. That is a TextProfile: a vocabulary and weights, plus whatever a corpus produced — a stopword set, a lemma map, a query-expansion network — plus the lineage saying how it was made.
prepare.jl fits one per corpus with TextSearch’s own textsearch fit, and not with this package’s fit_profile. The difference is what you get: fit_profile produces a vocabulary and weights, which is all an indexing corpus can yield on its own, while textsearch fit additionally runs an LSI over the corpus and derives a query-expansion network and a lemma map from it. Those artifacts are the reason the two query-side sections below demonstrate something instead of describing it.
The configuration used for every corpus is worth reading, because one line in it drives most of this page:
[normalization]
del_diac = false      # keep diacritics
lc = false            # keep case
del_punc = true
group_num = true
group_url = true
Keeping case and diacritics is a deliberate cost. Folding them is cheaper and gives a smaller vocabulary, and it is what the default TextConfig() does — but it also collapses leon and León into one token before the index ever sees them, which leaves the query side with nothing to work with. Everything in Correcting a query below exists only because these are false.

That is not an oversight, it is the distinction the type exists to make: computing an artifact and deciding to use it are different acts, and the second belongs to whoever indexes with the profile. Stopwords are applied because the vocabulary was counted with them already removed — un-applying those would mean refitting.

Installing, listing and describing profiles
This tutorial loads profiles from plain files on disk, with load_profile(path), because that needs nothing installed and keeps every path in this page explicit. For day-to-day use TextSearch’s CLI manages a profile library under ~/.textsearch/profiles/ instead:
textsearch install tutorials/profiles/gutenberg-es.zip gutenberg-es   # copy in under a nickname
textsearch install tutorials/profiles/gutenberg-es.zip                # nickname defaults to the filename
textsearch list                                                       # what is installed
textsearch info gutenberg-es                                          # vocabulary, artifacts, lineage
textsearch uninstall gutenberg-es                                     # reports what it *would* delete
textsearch uninstall gutenberg-es --force                             # actually deletes it
The nickname is a positional argument, not a flag, and defaults to the zip’s filename. Note what uninstall does without --force: it prints the path, the size and the command that would delete it, and removes nothing. Here the registration is the file — a profile can represent hours of compute and the installed copy may be the only one left — so the destructive reading of the word has to be asked for.
Once installed, a nickname works anywhere a path does in the CLI’s own commands. The file itself sits at ~/.textsearch/profiles/<nickname>.zip (or under $TEXTSEARCH_HOME), and load_profile takes that path like any other. Nothing below depends on having installed anything.

If a dictionary entry outranked the novel you were expecting, that is the corpus and the scoring function telling you something true. Neither the index nor the profile is misbehaving — a corpus assembled by popularity is simply not a corpus assembled for retrieval, and this is what that looks like before anyone filters it.

text:
Correcting a query
Because the profiles keep case and diacritics, a Spanish query typed without accents is not the same query the corpus contains. QueryPolicy’s default handles that, and can explain itself:


query: la musica del corazon
  ~ musica is in 9 documents against música's 724, so it reads as a misspelling; searched as música (variant), Música (variant) instead

query: el pais y la republica
  ~ republica is in 3 documents against República's 307, so it reads as a misspelling; searched as República (variant), república (variant) instead



Each line is a token the search replaced, with the evidence for replacing it. A correction happens only where the evidence says the typed spelling is wrong — it is absent from the vocabulary, or far rarer than another spelling of the same word. A correctly typed query produces no lines at all:


ftexplain on a correctly typed query: String[]

text:
Expanding a query
The expansion network relates each vocabulary token to its nearest neighbours in the LSI space the fit computed. prepare.jl turns it on when it creates each project — fit leaves it carried, and applying it is the indexer’s decision:
base = load_profile("tutorials/profiles/wikipedia-en.zip")
prof = TextSearch.with_applied(base; query_expansion=true)
create_project(dir, "wikipedia-en"; index_type=BM25InvertedFile, textmodel=BaseProfile(prof))
What the network holds for a few terms:


anarchism    -> anarchist, capitalism, individualist, Individualist, anarcho, anarchists
philosophy   -> metaphysics, philosophical, epistemology, Immanuel, Sramana, Sramanas
revolution   -> revolutions, Enlightenment, revolutionary, monde, mentalités, autonomy

title: Paragraph search over books and Wikipedia
text:
Building a project from scratch
Everything above opened projects prepare.jl had already built. Here is the whole path, live, on a small slice — this is what prepare.jl does, minus the scale:

slice = map(Iterators.take(eachline(corpus_file("gutenberg-en")), 2000)) do line
    o = JSON3.read(line)
    meta = Dict{String,Any}(String(k) => v for (k, v) in pairs(o) if k !== :text && k !== :doc_id)
    SSE.TextItem(String(o.text); doc_id=String(o.doc_id), meta)   # typed in, typed out
end

workdir = mktempdir()
h = SSE.create_project(workdir, "slice";
        index_type = TextSearch.BM25InvertedFile,
        textmodel  = SSE.BaseProfile(profiles["gutenberg-en"]))

SSE.append_items!(h, slice)          # stages: durable, but nothing is searchable yet
isempty(SSE.ftsearch(h, "the whale", 3))

true



quiet() do                           # see the note below on the engine's progress log
    SSE.index!(h)                    # encodes and indexes the backlog
end
[r.doc_id for r in SSE.ftsearch(h, "the whale", 3)]

3-element Vector{String}:
 "gutenberg-en-2701-p576"
 "gutenberg-en-2701-p1200"
 "gutenberg-en-2701-p775"


quiet there is this page’s own helper, redirect_stderr(devnull) do … end. Every index kind installs an InformativeLog that reports insertion progress on stderr, which is the right default for a build that runs for an hour and the wrong one for a document. Nothing about it is configurable through create_project; redirecting the stream is how you turn it off.
The split between the two cells is the engine’s staging model: append_items! makes an item durable immediately and searchable never; index! is the explicit, idempotent step that makes it searchable. It is why the first cell finds nothing and the second finds everything, and it is what lets a caller decide when to pay for indexing.
Reusing a profile a project already fitted is the same two lines in the other direction:

TextSearch.save_profile(joinpath(workdir, "exported"), SSE.text_profile(h))
reloaded = TextSearch.load_profile(joinpath(workdir, "exported"))



exported vocabulary: 136,716 tokens



The two alternatives, and why this page takes neither
Every project on this page was created from a BaseProfile, because prepare.jl had just fitted the profile and held it in hand. The other two forms matter more for a project you are starting from nothing.
DefaultProfile is the one to reach for, and it is what this page would use if it were not building its own profiles as it goes:
create_project(workdir, "noticias"; index_type=BM25InvertedFile,
               textmodel=DefaultProfile(:es))
At the first index! call it loads the published Spanish paragraph profile — the same wiki20231101-es-paragraphs this tutorial’s own fits are modelled on — and refits it against whatever you staged: counts blended, weights recomputed, stopwords and lemmas and the expansion network inherited. It resolves from the profile library textsearch install maintains, and says how to install the profile if it is not there.
The refit narrows the vocabulary to your corpus rather than keeping the language’s: measured on the English base, 335,336 tokens become 12,238 against an 800-document sample. What it buys is calibration and artifacts, not coverage; refit=false keeps the base whole if coverage is what you are after. DefaultProfile’s docstring has the numbers.
FitFromCorpus says, deliberately, that there is no pre-fitted model and one should be fitted from the project’s own corpus:
create_project(workdir, "self-fitted"; index_type=BM25InvertedFile,
               textmodel=FitFromCorpus(TextConfig(language=:en); min_ndocs=3, stopwords=0.9))
There is no default among the three, and the reason is a trap. That fit is delegated whole to TextSearch.fit_profile, which has no cheap variant — it always runs the LSI, the expansion network and the lemma clustering — so it is bounded by max_documents (1,000 by default) instead of by the corpus. Which means its vocabulary is fitted from a sample: every term appended later that the sample never held is out-of-vocabulary and silently dropped, forever. Nothing about the project’s behaviour afterwards distinguishes “I chose this” from “I never said”, which is exactly why it cannot be arrived at by omission — create_project refuses a text project with no textmodel.
The profiles table above is what that trap costs in the other direction: the four fits on this page took 129 to 863 seconds each, on corpora of 41,000 to 305,000 paragraphs. That is the price of a real profile, paid once, by a script — and the reason a project should be handed one rather than asked to produce it during its first index!.

Three things in that table are worth naming.
Incremental persistence is cheap, and the first project pays for the whole run. Every push_item! reports an :add! event and the project’s callback writes that paragraph’s encoded object to RocksDB as its own record, which sounds expensive and is not: measured warm on 3,000 paragraphs, the raw TextSearch push loop takes 0.08 ms per paragraph and the engine’s index! takes 0.129 — 1.6× for durability at every step.
The index! column is worth reading with that in mind, because the first row is not comparable with the others. Julia compiles the indexing path on its first execution, and the first project built absorbs all of it: an earlier measurement here reported thirty times the library’s cost per paragraph, and it was measuring compilation. The lesson generalises past this table — the first timing in a fresh Julia session is a compilation measurement wearing a throughput measurement’s clothes.
A search hit carries an id and a score, and nothing else. ftsearch answers with [SearchResult]s — _id, doc_id, distance, deleted — and getting from there to the paragraph means one fetch_items call per hit, as show_hits above does. That is one metadata read and one payload read per result, and a caller displaying a page of ten hits pays for ten of each.
Writing this page is what found that: the first version of it could not print a paragraph at all. fetch_items used to return a Dict{String,Any} of the record merged with its metadata, and the paragraph was in neither — text was a reserved key, stripped on the way in — so the page reached through handle.engine.staged[…] into a private field. Both halves are fixed now: fetch_items returns a typed StoredItem whose payload is the indexed text or vector, read through the public IndexEngine.stored_payload.
Creating a project against a large profile writes the whole profile into it. The create column is not project setup; it is the profile being serialised into the project’s own store so that reopening needs nothing but the project directory. That is the right default — a project that depends on a file somewhere else is a project that breaks when the file moves — but it does mean a shared profile is stored once per project that uses it.

title: Getting started
text:
by: Eric S. Téllez
This tutorial walks through the embedded API end to end, using paragraphs from Frankenstein (bundled in this package’s own test data) as a single running example: dense vector search with LSI-derived embeddings, full-text search with BM25 and TF-IDF, soft deletes, filtering, calibrating for a target recall, closing/reopening a project, and the “expensive”, whole-dataset operations (allknn, fft, closestpairs, bichromatic_kclosestpairs) that only make sense once you actually have a project’s worth of data to run them against. For a shorter, bare-minimum first look, see the repository’s README.

title: Getting started
text:
Installation
SimilaritySearchEngine.jl isn’t registered yet — develop it from a local checkout (or a git URL) alongside its own dependencies:
using Pkg
Pkg.develop(path="path/to/SimilaritySearchEngine.jl")

title: Getting started
text:
The Frankenstein dataset
This package’s own test suite ships test/data/frankenstein.jsonl — one JSON object per paragraph of the novel, already split, cleaned, and annotated by test/generate_datasets.jl. Loading it gives you a Vector of plain Dicts, each already shaped to match Schema.MetadataRecord’s record/data/metadata contract:
using JSON

items = [JSON.parse(l) for l in readlines("test/data/frankenstein.jsonl")]
length(items)  # 724 paragraphs
first(keys(items[1]))
Each item has:

"text": the paragraph itself (raw data — never duplicated into metadata).
"doc_id": an external id like "frankenstein_1" (the record’s fixed external-id field).
"keywords": character names detected in that paragraph, e.g. ["Elizabeth", "Victor"] (the record’s fixed, indexed tag field).
"ref": the previous paragraph’s doc_id (the record’s fixed, unvalidated reference field — a forward/backward link, here used to keep narrative order available even though nothing enforces refs point at something that exists).
"word_count"/"verb_count": free-form metadata (meta) — anything not a reserved key (vector/text/doc_id/keywords/ref) falls through here as-is, flat, with no wrapper key of its own.

There’s no "vector" key yet — that’s the dense section’s job, below.

title: Getting started
text:
Dense vectors with LSI (SearchGraph)
create_project makes a brand-new project directly on disk, at <workdir>/<dataset>. By default it builds a SearchGraph (an approximate, self-tuning index) autotuning toward minrecall=0.9:
using SimilaritySearchEngine
using SimilaritySearch: SearchGraph

workdir = mktempdir()
h = create_project(workdir, "frankenstein_dense"; index_type=SearchGraph, minrecall=0.9)

Getting real dense vectors quickly, with LSI
A SearchGraph project needs Vector{Float32}s to index — if you don’t already have an embedding model at hand, TextSearch.jl’s Latent Semantic Indexing (LSI) gives you real, meaningful dense vectors straight from a text corpus, in-process, with no external model or API call: fit once on your corpus, then project any text (an indexed paragraph, or a brand-new query) into that same dense space.
using TextSearch: LatentSemanticIndexing, outdim
using TextSearch.LSI: vectorize

corpus = [it["text"] for it in items]
lsi = LatentSemanticIndexing(corpus; maxoutdim=128, verbose=false)
outdim(lsi)  # 128 -- the full corpus easily supports it
(maxoutdim is a cap, not a guarantee: outdim(lsi) is min(maxoutdim, vocabulary size, corpus size) — a tiny placeholder corpus of just a handful of documents would yield far fewer dimensions than requested; 724 real paragraphs comfortably reach 128.)
Items are appended as a Vector of dicts, each carrying a "vector" key plus the record fields loaded above. We’ll only insert the first half of the book here, and hold the second half back in reserve, unindexed, for the bichromatic example further down:
half = length(items) ÷ 2

batch = [
    DenseItem(vectorize(lsi, it["text"]);
              doc_id = it["doc_id"], keywords = it["keywords"], refs = it["ref"],
              meta = Dict{String,Any}("word_count" => it["word_count"],
                                      "verb_count" => it["verb_count"]))
    for it in items[1:half]
]
append_items!(h, batch)  # inserted == 362
(append_items! accepts a batch — passing many items in one call amortizes better than one append_items! call per item, though both work; see Architecture for why batch size matters even more for a dense project specifically.)


Indexing the staged vectors
For a SearchGraph project, append_items! only stages raw vectors — cheaply, and durably, but without doing any of the (expensive) graph-connection work. Nothing is searchable yet:
search(h, vectorize(lsi, "the monster and its creator"), 5)  # Vector{...}[] -- empty, nothing indexed yet
index! explicitly builds the graph over whatever’s been staged since the last call (or since creation) — call it once you’re ready for staged items to become searchable, whether that’s right after every append_items! call, on your own periodic schedule, or just once before a batch of queries:
index!(h)
It’s cheap to call again later with nothing new staged (a no-op), and only ever processes the backlog — call it as often as fits your workflow. Searching now finds the 362 staged paragraphs:
query = vectorize(lsi, "the monster and its creator")
results = search(h, query, 5)
for r in results
    println(r.doc_id, " => distance ", r.distance)
end
Pass a filter predicate — a plain (record, meta) -> Bool function over each candidate’s fixed Schema.MetadataRecord (doc_id, keywords, refs, …) and its free-form meta (whatever else you appended it with) — to restrict results without building a separate query language:
mentions_someone = search(h, query, 5; filter = (record, meta) -> !isempty(record.keywords))


Soft deletes
delete_item! marks a document as logically deleted; the index itself is untouched. It takes the internal _id (the position add_item! assigned it, e.g. as returned in a search result’s doc_id field), not the "doc_id" you supplied when appending:
delete_item!(h, 1)  # internal _id 1, not any "doc_id"/metadata value

results = search(h, query, 5)
first(results).deleted  # true if internal _id 1 made the top-5 candidates
A soft-deleted candidate is reported, not hidden and backfilled — if you need k live results after filtering out deletions, overfetch and page yourself, or let SimilaritySearchServer’s cursor layer do it for you.


Calibrating for a target recall
calibrate! runs a real hyperparameter search and persists the result, so a later search(...; minrecall=0.95) call can serve that target recall from a tuned BeamSearch instead of the constructor’s default:
calibrate!(h; levels=[0.8, 0.9, 0.95, 0.97])
precise = search(h, query, 5; minrecall=0.95)
It needs a reasonably sized project to have anything meaningful to search against and tune over — this 724-paragraph corpus is plenty; a toy corpus of just a handful of items would print a wall of “ignoring configuration”/“too few queries” warnings instead (harmless, just noisy), since there wouldn’t be enough distinct items for its own internal sample queries.


Closing and reopening
close_project!(h)

h2 = open_project(workdir, "frankenstein_dense")
same_query_results = search(h2, query, 5)
close_project!(h2)
Every insertion was already persisted incrementally as it happened (see Architecture), so close_project! only needs to flush anything still pending for index kinds that don’t persist incrementally on their own. Staging and indexing are tracked separately, too: reopening restores exactly how far index! actually got, not just how much was staged – had we appended more items after the last index! call above and closed without indexing them, they’d still be there (staged, with their metadata already fetchable) after reopening, just not yet searchable, waiting on a future index! call to catch them up.
same_query_results will be close to, but isn’t guaranteed to be byte-identical to, the results from before closing: SearchGraph is an approximate index, and rebuilding it from persisted vectors (open_project replays every insertion in the same order) doesn’t guarantee an identical internal graph topology to the one built live, so its beam search can explore a slightly different candidate set — expect the same ballpark of hits (often exactly the same), not a bitwise-reproducible top-k, unless you calibrate and search with an explicit minrecall on both sides.

title: Getting started
text:
Full-text search with BM25
Text projects work the same way as dense ones, just with a "text" key instead of "vector", and ftsearch instead of search — and, since the redesign that decoupled staging from indexing, the exact same append_items!(stage)/index!(build) shape as a dense project, not a separate training step. BM25InvertedFile scores via BM25 over raw bags-of-words:
using TextSearch: BM25InvertedFile

# `textmodel` is required for a text project -- see the next section for what the
# alternative is and why neither is a default
hb = create_project(workdir, "frankenstein_bm25"; index_type=BM25InvertedFile,
                    textmodel=FitFromCorpus())

append_items!(hb, [
    TextItem(it["text"]; doc_id = it["doc_id"], keywords = it["keywords"])
    for it in items[1:200]
])  # only stages raw text -- nothing searchable yet

index!(hb)  # first call: fits the TextProfile from everything staged so far, then indexes it

hits = ftsearch(hb, "monster creature fear", 5)
for r in hits
    println(r.doc_id, " => distance ", r.distance)
end

close_project!(hb)
index!’s first call on a text project doubles as training: it fits a TextProfile (vocabulary, tf-idf weights, lineage) and builds the real BM25InvertedFile from every item staged so far, then encodes/indexes that same backlog — there’s no separate training entry point or “must be trained first” error. Every later index! call just catches up whatever’s been staged since, exactly like the dense case: idempotent, safe to call repeatedly, a cheap no-op when nothing new is staged.
Tokens never seen at that first index! call are out-of-vocabulary on every later append and silently dropped, so what you’ve staged before it has to be representative of the text you’ll keep appending. text_profile(hb) hands you the fitted model, and save_profile writes it out for reuse — but the real fix for a project that keeps growing is the next section.

title: Getting started
text:
Choosing the text model
textmodel above was not decoration. Creating a text project requires it, and there is no default:
create_project(workdir, "oops"; index_type=BM25InvertedFile)
# ERROR: a text project (BM25InvertedFile) needs an explicit `textmodel`, because the ways to
#        get a vocabulary are not interchangeable and the cheap one cannot be undone later: ...
Three forms answer where the vocabulary comes from. They are not variations on one setting, and the order below is the order worth preferring them in.

DefaultProfile — start from a language, adapt to your corpus
hes = create_project(workdir, "noticias"; index_type=BM25InvertedFile,
                     textmodel=DefaultProfile(:es))
This is the one to reach for. At the first index! call it loads the published Spanish paragraph profile and refits it against whatever you have staged: the base’s token counts are blended with your corpus’s, the weights recomputed, and the stopword set, lemma map and expansion network inherited. No embedding is fitted, which is what makes a refit cheap next to a fit.
Be clear about what the refit does and does not give you, because the obvious guess is wrong. Measured on the published English profile: 335,336 tokens in the base, 12,238 after refitting against an 800-document sample, of which 2,649 are tokens the sample never held. Fitting on that sample alone would have given 9,589. So the refit narrows to your corpus’s vocabulary, widened about a quarter by the base — it is not language-wide coverage. What you inherit is the part your own corpus cannot produce: weights calibrated over millions of paragraphs, and (for that base) 96 stopwords, 16,661 lemmas and 10,655 expansion entries.
If coverage is what you need — terms a later batch will introduce that today’s corpus has never seen — pass refit=false and index against the base untouched, all 335,336 tokens, with Wikipedia’s weights rather than yours. Calibration or coverage: the two forms answer different questions.
The profile is resolved from the library textsearch install maintains, under ~/.textsearch/profiles/. Nothing is bundled or downloaded — the profiles are 70–160 MB — and if the one you asked for is not installed the error says so and prints the command that installs it. refit=false indexes against the base untouched, and nickname= points at any installed profile instead of the per-language default.


FitFromCorpus — deliberately no base profile
Fit the model from this project’s own staged corpus, at the first index! call. This is the explicit way to say “I have nothing pre-fitted”, and it is the weakest of the three:
using TextSearch: NormalizationConfig

hf = create_project(workdir, "noticias_propias"; index_type=BM25InvertedFile,
    textmodel=FitFromCorpus(TextConfig(normalization=NormalizationConfig(lc=false, del_diac=false),
                                       language=:es);
                            min_ndocs=3, stopwords=0.9))
Its argument is the corpus-independent policy — normalization, tokenization, and the language the corpus is in. The default TextConfig() lowercases and strips diacritics, which is usually right for English and throws away a distinction that matters in Spanish.
The fit itself is handed whole to TextSearch.fit_profile; this package does not fit profiles. That has a consequence worth stating plainly: there is no cheap variant of that pipeline. Every fit runs an LSI over the sample, derives an expansion network from it and clusters a lemma map from the same embeddings. Measured on 3,000 paragraphs it takes about 49 seconds, against 0.2 for a bare vocabulary-and-weights pass — which is why max_documents exists:







option
what it does




max_documents
read at most this many documents (1,000 by default), sampled by an even stride across the corpus rather than taken from the front. 0 lifts the cap


min_ndocs
drop a token seen in fewer documents than this, before the encoder runs. Not cosmetic: the expansion network is an all-pairs kNN over the vocabulary


stopwords
a document-frequency threshold in (0, 1]; tokens above it are dropped and the vocabulary recounted without them. A second pass over the sample


encoder, expansion, lemmas
the library’s own option groups, as NamedTuples — encoder=(; outdim=128), lemmas=(; apply=true)



The cap bounds the cost and cuts against the one thing this path is already worst at: a vocabulary from 1,000 sampled documents is thin, so more of what you append later is out-of-vocabulary and silently dropped. That is the trade, and it is why the section above exists.


BaseProfile — a model fitted elsewhere
hp = create_project(workdir, "noticias_wiki"; index_type=BM25InvertedFile,
                    textmodel=BaseProfile(load_profile("wiki20231101-es.zip")))
This trains the project before its first item is ever staged, and is what DefaultProfile does underneath once it has resolved and refitted — use this form when you already hold the file, or when you want the base used exactly as it is. To load a profile but decline one of its artifacts, change the profile rather than the project: BaseProfile(with_applied(p; lemmas=false)).
Either way the spec is persisted with the project and restored verbatim by open_project. And a project that fitted its own model can export it for the next one to index against:
save_profile("mi-perfil", text_profile(hes))
create_project(workdir, "hermano"; index_type=BM25InvertedFile,
               textmodel=BaseProfile(load_profile("mi-perfil")))
Passing a textmodel to a dense project is an error rather than an ignored keyword — there is no reading under which it does anything.

title: Getting started
text:
Correcting and widening a query
A query travels with a QueryPolicy, because whether to correct a misspelling or widen a search is a guess about what the person meant — a property of the query, not of the index:
ftsearch(hes, "musica clasica", 5)                                   # :auto (the default)
ftsearch(hes, "musica clasica", 5; policy=QueryPolicy(correction=:off))   # exactly as typed
Under :auto, a typed token is bridged to another spelling of the same word only where the evidence says the typed one is wrong — it is absent from the vocabulary, or far rarer than another spelling of it. On a corpus indexed with del_diac=false, musica reaches música and clasica reaches clásica; a correctly typed query is left alone. Under the default TextConfig() this is inert, since folding case and diacritics already collapsed those spellings into one.
A search that silently substitutes what was asked for owes the caller a way to see it, which is ftexplain:
julia> ftexplain(hes, "musica clasica")
2-element Vector{String}:
 "musica is in 1 document against música's 60, so it reads as a misspelling; searched as música (variant) instead"
 "clasica is in 1 document against clásica's 60, so it reads as a misspelling; searched as clásica (variant) instead"
QueryPolicy also carries expansion/expansion_k, which widen the query with the profile’s query-expansion network — inert unless the project was created from a profile that carries one.

title: Getting started
text:
Full-text search with TF-IDF
TextInvertedFile is the other text index kind: a classic TF-IDF-weighted (IdfWeighting + TfWeighting) inverted index, cosine distance by default — a good baseline to compare against BM25’s ranking on the same corpus. (InvertedFile selects the same engine and is accepted interchangeably; TextInvertedFile is the name of what actually gets built.)
using TextSearch: TextInvertedFile

ht = create_project(workdir, "frankenstein_tfidf"; index_type=TextInvertedFile,
                    textmodel=FitFromCorpus())

append_items!(ht, [
    TextItem(it["text"]; doc_id = it["doc_id"], keywords = it["keywords"])
    for it in items[1:200]
])

index!(ht)  # same stage-then-index shape as BM25 above

hits = ftsearch(ht, "monster creature fear", 5)
for r in hits
    println(r.doc_id, " => distance ", r.distance)
end

close_project!(ht)
Same insertion/search shape as BM25 — only index_type changes — so switching between the two to compare rankings on your own corpus is a one-line change.

title: Getting started
text:
Expensive, whole-dataset operations
allknn, fft, closestpairs, and bichromatic_kclosestpairs all run synchronously, in-process — no job queue, unlike the HTTP API’s POST /api/v1/jobs/allknn — which is exactly why they’re grouped here as their own section: each one does real work proportional to the whole dataset (or two datasets, for the bichromatic case), so run them against a project you actually want an answer for, not casually inside a hot loop. All four need a dense (SearchGraph) project; reopen the one from the LSI section above if you closed it:
h2 = open_project(workdir, "frankenstein_dense")

All-pairs nearest neighbors
allknn runs SimilaritySearch.jl’s batch all-nearest-neighbors — every item’s own top-k neighbors, all at once:
neighbors = allknn(h2; k=5)
first(neighbors)  # (id=1, neighbors=[...], dists=[...])
id/neighbors are internal _ids (1-based insertion position), not doc_ids — see Metadata lookups to resolve them back to paragraph text.


Farthest-first traversal (diverse sampling)
fft picks k items that are as far from each other as possible — useful for a diverse, representative sample of the corpus (e.g. candidate cluster centers), rather than the “closest to a query” shape every other search here has:
R = fft(h2, 8; verbose=false)
R.centers  # 8 well-separated internal _ids
R.ε        # the separation radius achieved


k closest pairs (near-duplicates and echoes within one corpus)
closestpairs finds the k globally closest pairs of items within a single project — useful for spotting near-duplicate or strongly echoing passages:
pairs = closestpairs(h2; k=5)
for (i, j, d) in pairs
    ri = get_metadata(h2.project, i)
    rj = get_metadata(h2.project, j)
    println(ri.doc_id, " <-> ", rj.doc_id, "  dist=", d)
    println("  A: ", first(items[i]["text"], 90))
    println("  B: ", first(items[j]["text"], 90))
end
Running this against the first half of the novel (h2 as built above) turns up passages like Elizabeth’s account of Justine’s trial echoed a few paragraphs later almost verbatim, at a distance well below typical unrelated pairs — exactly the kind of near-duplicate/ strong echo this function is for.


Bichromatic k closest pairs (across two collections)
bichromatic_kclosestpairs finds the k closest pairs between a project’s own index and a second, separate collection of vectors that isn’t indexed by anything — here, the first half of the novel (already indexed as h2, see above) against the second half’s vectors (computed with the same LSI model, but never inserted anywhere):
using SimilaritySearch: MatrixDatabase

second_half_vectors = [vectorize(lsi, it["text"]) for it in items[(half + 1):end]]
B = MatrixDatabase(hcat(second_half_vectors...))

pairs = bichromatic_kclosestpairs(h2, B; k=5)
for (i, j, d) in pairs
    ri = get_metadata(h2.project, i)             # i is h2's own internal _id
    other = items[half + j]                       # j is B's own 1-based position
    println(ri.doc_id, " <-> ", other["doc_id"], "  dist=", d)
    println("  A: ", first(items[i]["text"], 100))
    println("  B: ", first(other["text"], 100))
end
On the real novel, this surfaces thematically matched passages across the two halves — e.g. Walton’s opening framing letters about a “strange accident” pairing with an equally breathless first-person account much later in the book, well below the distance of an unrelated cross-half pair.

title: Getting started
text:
Metadata lookups
fetch_items and exists accept either the internal _id (an integer, or a string of one, e.g. "1") or the doc_id you supplied when appending. fetch_items returns a StoredItem per resolved id — the record’s fixed fields, its free-form meta, and the payload that was actually indexed:
it = only(fetch_items(h2, ["frankenstein_2"]))
it._id            # 2
it.doc_id         # "frankenstein_2"
it.keywords       # ["Chapter", ...]
it.meta["word_count"]
it.payload        # the vector this project indexed (a paragraph, in a text project)

exists(h2, [1, "some-doc-id"])   # Vector{ExistsResult}: (id, exists, deleted)
An id that resolves to nothing is dropped by fetch_items (so the result can be shorter than what you asked for) and reported by exists (so it is always the same length).
get_metadata(h2.project, _id) (used in the closest-pairs examples above) is the lower-level single-record accessor fetch_items itself is built on — it returns just the Schema.MetadataRecord (no meta merged in), which is all those examples needed.

title: SimilaritySearchEngine.jl
text: SimilaritySearchEngine.jl is an embedded, no-HTTP-required Julia API for running similarity search projects: named, persistent collections of dense vectors or text documents backed by SimilaritySearch.jl, TextSearch.jl, and RocksDB.jl. A script does using SimilaritySearchEngine and calls its functions directly — no running server, no CLI subprocess, no job queue. The trust boundary is just OS file permissions on a working directory, the same as any other embedded database.

title: SimilaritySearchEngine.jl
text:
What it gives you

Project lifecycle: create_project, open_project, close_project! manage a project’s on-disk RocksDB directory and the live search engine backing it.
Dense vector search over a SearchGraph (an approximate, self-tuning graph index), or an exact ExhaustiveSearch/ParallelExhaustiveSearch, all sharing the same append_items!/search surface — for a SearchGraph, append_items! only stages raw vectors, and the (expensive) graph-connection step happens in a separate, explicit index! call, so a caller controls when that cost is paid.
Full-text search over a BM25InvertedFile or a weighted TextInvertedFile, sharing the same append_items!(stage)/index!(build)/ftsearch surface as the dense case — the first index! call on a text project also fits its TextProfile from whatever’s been staged so far, so there’s no separate training step to call first.
A text model stated explicitly: creating a text project requires a textmodel, and there is no default. Prefer DefaultProfile(:es) — the published profile for a language, refitted to your own corpus at the first index! call, so your weights are calibrated over millions of paragraphs and the stopwords, lemmas and query-expansion network are inherited rather than derived (refit=false keeps the base’s language-wide vocabulary instead). BaseProfile(p) uses a profile you already hold. FitFromCorpus(TextConfig(language=:es)) is the explicit “no base profile” escape, delegated to TextSearch.fit_profile and capped at max_documents to bound its cost — which makes its vocabulary thin, and that is not a decision to arrive at by omission. Queries then travel with a QueryPolicy: whether to correct their spelling against the vocabulary (ftexplain reports what was corrected, correction=:off undoes it) and whether to widen them with the profile’s expansion network.
Typed in, typed out: items are DenseItem/TextItem values and results are SearchResult/StoredItem/ExistsResult. No JSON-shaped dictionary is taken apart by key name on the way in or assembled on the way out; meta stays a free-form Dict{String,Any}, and get_raw_meta is the one raw path, reserved for the HTTP server.
Soft deletes: delete_item! marks a document as logically deleted without touching the underlying index; search reports a deleted marker per candidate instead of silently hiding or backfilling it.
Recall calibration: calibrate! runs SimilaritySearch.jl’s real hyperparameter search so later queries can ask for minrecall=0.95 (or any other target) and get back a BeamSearch tuned for it.
Whole-dataset operations: allknn, fft (diverse sampling), closestpairs (near-duplicate detection), and bichromatic_kclosestpairs (closest pairs across two collections) all run synchronously, in-process, against a dense project’s index.
Incremental, per-field persistence: every mutation writes only the storage it actually touched — a SearchGraph’s raw vectors go straight into a memory-mapped file, a soft delete never rewrites the index, and routine inserts never rewrite the whole engine state. See Architecture for the on-disk layout.

title: SimilaritySearchEngine.jl
text:
Where this fits
This package is deliberately scoped to project lifecycle, core CRUD, calibration, and the whole-dataset operations (allknn, fft, closestpairs, bichromatic_kclosestpairs) — every function here mirrors an existing code path in the sibling SimilaritySearchServer package (same on-disk layout, same insertion/search/persistence semantics), so a project touched through this embedded API stays fully interoperable with SimilaritySearchServer’s CLI and HTTP server. Development happens here first, at the engine level, and is ported to SimilaritySearchServer afterwards.
